Page at 0.0365 outranks every wood species on the page.

Type resolution is poor where it matters commercially. White Oak and Hickory both resolve to LOCATION rather than a material or product type, and American resolves to LOCATION mapped to the United States — which is defensible for the brand's made-in-USA positioning but not for the product name "American Scrape Oak". Hard Maple, which the Species facet confirms is in stock, does not surface as an entity at all because the editorial prose never mentions maple.

The gap: no typed entity anchors this page to a flooring product category, and the 372 words of filter chrome are actively competing with the 502 words of prose for salience share.

What Works

Signal: US11409748B1 treats the H1→H2→H3 path as a vector matched against query intent. A single unambiguous H1 with the head term in it, and H2s that read like the questions a buyer actually asks, is the condition this system rewards. Passage-level indexing can lift the "Choosing the Right Hand-Scraped Wood Floor" block on its own for selection-intent queries.

  • Single, keyword-aligned H1 with a clean editorial heading spine. The HTML audit records exactly one H1, "Hand Scraped Hardwood Flooring \| Handscraped Floors On Sale", followed by a coherent descent through "All About The Hand-Scraped Hardwood Floor", "A Unique Hardwood Flooring Touch" and "Choosing the Right Hand-Scraped Wood Floor".

Signal: Correct self-referencing identifiers are what lets Google bind the structured data to this URL rather than discarding it as ambiguous, and an accurate BreadcrumbList is the direct input to breadcrumb display in the SERP. This is the schema layer done right, which makes the missing commerce nodes a gap rather than a failure.

  • CollectionPage and BreadcrumbList are implemented correctly, not just present. The CollectionPage node self-references this exact URL on both @id and url, carries datePublished and dateModified, and nests a three-step breadcrumb (Home, Products, Handscraped) that mirrors the visible trail.

Signal: Nothing is stranded from the crawl, so link equity and index coverage reach all 24 SKUs. Internally consistent counts also mean the underlying product data is sound — which isolates the credibility problem on this page to the editorial copy alone, not the catalogue.

  • Full inventory is crawlable and the facet layer is internally consistent. The grid states "Items 1 - 12 of 24" with pagination exposing the second page, and every facet group independently sums to the full 24: Species at 11 + 2 + 6 + 5, Grade at 19 + 3 + 2, Width at 18 + 5 + 1, Type at 18 + 6, Location at 6 + 18.

Signal: High percentBodyTitleTokensCovered is the measure Goldmine uses to decide whether a title is honest about its page. Strong coverage plus readable phrasing keeps isBadTitle off and suppresses rewrite pressure.

  • Title tag is well formed for Goldmine. 59 characters, primary keyword at the start, natural language, and every substantive title token recurs in the body, breadcrumb or navigation.

What Could Be Improved

Fix: Rewrite to match the catalogue: state the first-quality entry price and the overall entry price separately, for example that hand-scraped solids start at $7.00 sq ft in 1st Quality while Blue Label engineered starts at $1.99 sq ft. Pulling the two apart costs nothing and converts a contradiction into a genuine value story about grades, which is a differentiator no competitor page carries.

  • The lead price claim contradicts the page's own grade facet. The prose closes its buying advice with "And these first quality hardwood floors are available for a price as low as $1.99 sq ft." — but the only $1.99 products on the page are both graded "Blue Label", and the Grade facet separates "1st Quality (19)" from "Blue Label (3)" as distinct grades. The cheapest floors on this page are, by the site's own classification, not first quality.

Fix: Reconcile the bucket boundaries to the real price distribution and close the gaps — $1.00 - $1.99, $2.00 - $2.99, $7.00 - $7.99 — then regenerate the counts and align the prose claim to whichever figure survives. Adjacent bands with dead zones between them are a merchandising bug a shopper hits on the first filter click.

  • The price facet advertises a bucket the copy says does not exist, and the two visible $1.99 products fall into the gap between buckets. The facet offers "$1.00 - $1.98 (3)" against prose claiming "as low as $1.99 sq ft" — one of the two is wrong. Separately, the buckets run $1.00 - $1.98 then $2.00 - $2.98, so a product priced exactly $1.99 (two of them are visible in the grid) is not selectable through any price band on the page.

Fix: Delete the Douglas fir sentence and spend the words on Hard Maple, which is actually purchasable here. Recommending unstocked inventory on a commercial category page invites the immediate bounce back to the SERP that badClicks measures, and a recommendation the catalogue cannot honour is exactly the mismatch quality systems are built to detect.

  • The copy recommends a wood species the page does not stock. The prose says "Consider hand-scraped Douglas fir for a distinctive grain pattern that adds depth and warmth to any space." The Species facet lists "Hickory (11)", "Hard Maple (2)", "Oak (6)" and "White Oak (5)" — four values summing to all 24 SKUs, so there is no fir anywhere in this collection, on either page of the grid. Conversely Hard Maple is in stock and is never mentioned in the prose.

Fix: Emit an ItemList wrapping Product nodes with Offer and price for each of the 24 SKUs, and an AggregateOffer with lowPrice and highPrice at collection level. On a site whose entire positioning is price, leaving every price invisible to structured extraction is the single highest-leverage technical fix on this page.

  • 24 priced products are rendered with zero commerce schema. JSON-LD covers CollectionPage, BreadcrumbList, WebSite and SiteNavigationElement, but there is no ItemList, no Product, no Offer and no AggregateOffer — so price, grade, width, species and availability exist only as pixels.

Fix: Cut the repetitions back to natural density and reinvest the space in the specification vocabulary the page is missing entirely. Consider adding terms like: janka hardness rating, wear layer thickness, plank thickness, finish type, underlayment, radiant heat compatibility, acclimation period, square feet per carton, warranty length. That raises depth and closes the expectedTf gap in one edit rather than two.

  • The head term is stuffed in reversed word order, and the page is the thinnest of the nine. At 502 editorial prose words this page sits at the bottom of a set running to 2,324, and hand-scraped variants appear roughly eighteen times inside those 502 words, producing inversions such as "With our diverse flooring hand-scraped inventory, you'll discover options that blend rustic charm with modern convenience."

Fix: Repoint the pagination anchors at the product grid container (the page already exposes a "Skip to product list" target for this purpose), add og:title, og:description, og:image and twitter:card using the hero product image, and trim the meta description below 160 characters while keeping the price hook.

  • Pagination links point at a fragment that does not exist, and social metadata is absent. Every pagination link targets the fragment #customer-review-list, which appears nowhere in the DOM, while the page carries zero Open Graph tags and zero Twitter Card tags and a meta description of 164 characters that will truncate.

Verdict

Correct Entity placement, a clean single-H1 heading spine and a properly self-referencing CollectionPage with an accurate breadcrumb hold this page at a functional baseline, but Content Quality and Salient Terms both flag Weak: 502 editorial words is the thinnest in the set, the head term is repeated in machine-reversed word order, and three separate merchandising claims contradict the page's own facet data — the first-quality price claim against "Blue Label (3)", the "as low as $1.99 sq ft" claim against the "$1.00 - $1.98 (3)" bucket, and a Douglas fir recommendation against a Species facet that accounts for all 24 SKUs without it. Schema scores Adequate rather than Strong for one reason: 24 priced SKUs and not a single Product, Offer or ItemList node to expose them.

Would an AI Cite This Page?

Partially — the product data yes, the editorial prose no, and three of its sentences are contradicted by the page's own filter data.

The product grid is citable. Each of the twelve tiles carries atomic, attributable facts: a named product, a price, a width, a grade, a colour and a construction type. "American Scrape Hickory" at $7.75, in width 5, grade "1st Quality", "Color Name:" of "Clover Honey", type "Prefinished Solid" is exactly the shape of claim a retrieval system can quote and attribute. So is "Items 1 - 12 of 24", and so is every facet count — Hickory (11) against Oak (6), Prefinished Solid (18) against Engineered (6), Murphy, NC (6) against Dickson, TN (18). This is the retailer's own stock, so it has real retrieval uniqueness: no other page in the index holds it. For a query like cheapest hand scraped hickory hardwood per square foot, these numbers are the reason to surface this URL at all.

The 502 editorial words are the thinnest in the nine-page set — the set runs from 502 here to 2,324 at the deepest — and judged on that editorial figure, which excludes the product grid (primary content on an ecommerce category page, not padding) and the 372 words of filter and sort chrome (template furniture, credited as neither), the prose contains no number except one price, no source, no named authority, and no claim that could not be written about any hand-scraped floor sold anywhere. "Each hand-scraped floor is meticulously crafted to showcase the natural beauty and imperfections of the wood, making it a stunning addition to any room." is a textbook low-citation-probability signal from the framework: a generic statement whose embedding sits on top of millions of near-identical vectors. "There's an option for every home!" is hedging with no substance behind it.

The decisive problem is worse than thinness. Three editorial claims disagree with the live data the same page is rendering.

  • The prose says "Consider hand-scraped Douglas fir for a distinctive grain pattern that adds depth and warmth to any space." The Species filter on the same screen reads Hickory (11), Hard Maple (2), Oak (6), White Oak (5) — four species summing to exactly 24, which matches "Items 1 - 12 of 24" for the whole category. There is no Douglas fir in it.
  • The prose says "And these first quality hardwood floors are available for a price as low as $1.99 sq ft." The only two products on the page priced at $1.99 are "Pub Scrape Discontinued" and "Pub Scrape", and both are graded "Blue Label". Every one of the ten visible products graded "1st Quality" is priced at $7.00 or $7.75.
  • The prose says "When selecting the ideal hardwood floor, consider a product with wide plank boards. Wider planks will add a sense of grandeur to your room." The Width filter reads 5 (18), Random (5), 7 (1) — one product in twenty-four is wider than five inches.

A cross-encoder reranker scores the query against the chunk. When the chunk asserts a fact and the adjacent chunk from the same document refutes it, the document loses on the reranking criteria of relevance and information completeness at once, and the framework's trust anti-patterns apply directly. The page is not merely uncitable here; it supplies its own counter-evidence.

Retrieval & Chunking Quality

Chunking is dominated by UI, not by content. The HTML audit records ten H3 headings, and eight of them are filter labels — "Price filter", "Species filter", "Wear Layer filter", "Square Footage filter", "Location filter", "Width filter", "Grade filter", "Type filter". A chunker that splits on structural boundaries, as the framework describes, will therefore produce eight chunks whose heading context is a widget name and whose body is a list of counts. Only two H2 boundaries and one H3 in the entire page open an editorial passage.

The editorial headings that do exist are good. "All About The Hand-Scraped Hardwood Floor" and "Choosing the Right Hand-Scraped Wood Floor" are both descriptive, both front-load the distinguishing term, and both map to real query intents — the second is close to a verbatim match for how to choose hand scraped hardwood flooring. "A Unique Hardwood Flooring Touch" is weaker; it names no subject a reader could search for, and as standalone passage context it tells a retriever almost nothing.

Position is wrong for attention weighting. Every editorial word sits below the H1, below the whole Shop By filter rail, and below all twelve product tiles. The framework's position bias puts extra attention weight on the opening and closing of a document; here the opening is navigation and filter chrome, and the only substantive prose is buried in the back half. The one sentence on the page that a model would most want — "Hand-scraped hardwood flooring also offers a durability that you cannot get in a smooth surface, as the distressed finish helps to hide scratches and gouges that can change the appearance of your floor." — is in the last third of the second editorial block.

Sections are self-contained but shallow. Each editorial block is two to four paragraphs and does hold together as a unit, so chunks will not split mid-thought. The problem is that each resulting chunk carries roughly 150 to 200 words of unsourced generality, which is enough to be retrieved and not nearly enough to be preferred at rerank.

Embeddings will land correctly and then fail to differentiate. Google NLP returns /Home & Garden/Home Improvement/Flooring at 0.99 confidence, so first-pass vector search will treat this as a flooring page without hesitation. But the top entities by salience are "hardwood flooring", "Handscraped Floors On Sale" and "Scrape Oak Price", trailed by a run of widget entities — Page, Price filter, filter, Layer filter, Footage filter — so the filter chrome is contributing as much entity salience as the merchandise. The page is placed in the right semantic region and gives a retriever no reason to pick it out of that region.

What Works

RAG Impact: Chunking follows structural boundaries, so a descriptive heading means the chunk boundary and the query intent coincide. At rerank time a cross-encoder scores the query against the chunk including its heading, so a heading that restates the user's question is itself a relevance signal — where a heading like Overview or More Info would contribute nothing.

  • Two editorial H2 headings that are shaped like the questions people ask. "All About The Hand-Scraped Hardwood Floor" and "Choosing the Right Hand-Scraped Wood Floor" both front-load the topic term and describe a genuine subtopic rather than labelling a slot.

RAG Impact: The framework's first citation-selection criterion is a specific, factual claim — a number, a date, a name. These counts are nothing but that, and because they describe this retailer's own stock they carry the retrieval uniqueness that makes an LLM cite a commercial source instead of routing around it. That they all reconcile to the same total is what makes them safe to quote.

  • Facet counts that are internally consistent and describe the whole category. Every facet on the page sums to exactly 24, matching "Items 1 - 12 of 24": species as Hickory (11), Hard Maple (2), Oak (6), White Oak (5); type as Prefinished Solid (18) and Engineered (6); grade as 1st Quality (19), Blue Label (3), Builder A (2); warehouse as Murphy, NC (6) and Dickson, TN (18); footage as 0 - 1000 (20) and 1000 - 2000 (4).

RAG Impact: Retrieval operates on chunks a crawler can actually reach. Category inventory that exists only behind an unlinked reveal never enters the index at all; here the full set is addressable, so the whole catalogue for this category is available for chunking rather than only the first screen.

  • All 24 products are reachable, so no inventory is stranded from a crawler. The grid states "Items 1 - 12 of 24" and exposes a second page alongside "Show All Products" and "Show 12 more products" controls.

RAG Impact: This is the only sentence on the page that states a mechanism — texture conceals damage — rather than an adjective. It directly answers does hand scraped flooring hide scratches, which is a high-intent question, and it is phrased concisely enough to survive extraction as a quote. The framework's quotability criterion is met by this one sentence and by no other on the page.

  • One genuinely functional, citable claim about hand-scraping. "Hand-scraped hardwood flooring also offers a durability that you cannot get in a smooth surface, as the distressed finish helps to hide scratches and gouges that can change the appearance of your floor."

RAG Impact: This resolves the page to one unambiguous entity and places it in a hierarchy the retriever does not have to infer. Self-consistent @id and url also prevent the duplicate-entity confusion that scrambles attribution when a retrieval layer cannot tell which URL a chunk belongs to. This layer is done right and should be preserved exactly as it stands while the missing commercial nodes are added around it.

  • CollectionPage schema that identifies the page correctly, with a valid breadcrumb. The JSON-LD carries a CollectionPage node whose @id and url both self-reference https://www.reallycheapfloors.com/shop/hand-scraped-hardwood/, a name of "Handscraped", and a correct three-step BreadcrumbList of Home, then Products, then Handscraped. A second script declares the WebSite entity with a SearchAction.

RAG Impact: A 0.99 primary category means the embedding lands squarely in the flooring region with no dilution into adjacent verticals, so the page is a candidate in first-pass vector search. Full alt coverage closes the framework's image-only anti-pattern — alt text is the only channel through which a product photograph contributes anything retrievable at all.

  • Clean topical classification and no image-only information. Google NLP returns /Home & Garden/Home Improvement/Flooring at 0.99 confidence, and the HTML audit confirms all 23 images carry alt text.

Verdict

An LLM would quote this page's product grid and facet counts today and would not quote a sentence of its 502 editorial words, which are the thinnest in the set and which contradict the page's own filter data in three places — recommending Douglas fir that is not stocked, attaching a $1.99 price to "1st Quality" goods that start at $7.00, and advising wide planks where the Width filter reads 7 (1) for the entire wide-plank inventory. The single highest-value change is to rewrite those three claims from the live facet data, because a page that refutes itself gives a reranker a reason to drop it even when the underlying inventory data is unique and worth citing.

YMYL Classification

Not core YMYL. This is a commercial/transactional category page for building materials, which sits in the QRG's "Unlikely YMYL" band on topic alone. It is pulled toward the "May be YMYL" middle of the spectrum by the size of the purchase the page itself describes — it quotes an average of $3,162 to install new flooring in a standard 320-square-foot living room, and a wrong grade or sheen choice at that spend is a real financial consequence for a household. The practical implication for scoring: no medical-grade credentialing is required, but price accuracy is held to a stricter standard than it would be on a purely informational page, because price is the transaction term the buyer acts on. That is precisely where this page is weakest, which is why the contradictions below are weighted as trust findings rather than as copy-editing nits.

What Works

Why this matters (QRG): High-quality MC is defined by "effort, skill, and talent" and by "unique value or perspective". A liquidator explaining which of its own grades will disappoint a buyer is the opposite of content "written for search engines rather than humans".

  • The editorial layer is by far the deepest in the nine-page set, and it is original rather than padded. Judged on the editorial prose figure of 2,324 words — the 407 words of filter and sort chrome are template furniture and are not credited as depth — this page runs against a set that starts at 502 words at its thinnest. The prose earns the length: it carries a graded buying framework, a "Key Takeaways" block, five FAQ answers and a named-product price list under "Example picks (with real product page prices)", not a restated species description.

Why this matters (QRG): Trustworthiness is the central E-E-A-T element, and "honest intent" with "no deception, manipulation, or hidden agendas" is its core test. Disclosing a product's downside before purchase is direct evidence of that intent.

  • The page takes a position against its own short-term interest, which is a first-order trust signal. It warns buyers off a product it stocks — "Cabin grade can look awesome, but expect defects and short boards (it ain’t all pretty)." — and tells flippers "The floor is a tool, not jewelry." It also explains why a cheaper line exists rather than hiding the margin logic: "Buying our Blue Label cabin grade gives you the exact same material and finish as 1st Quality for a fraction of the cost."

Why this matters (QRG): Expertise indicators include "professional vocabulary used naturally (not forced for SEO)" and "content that educates rather than just restates common knowledge". Defining the unit is what separates demonstrated expertise from copied specification text.

  • Technical claims are specific, correct and explained, not dropped as jargon. "The Janka Hardness Scale rates it at 1290 lbf" is the accepted figure for red oak, and the page immediately unpacks the unit rather than leaving it as an authority prop. It then places the species in context: "This rating is a bit softer than white oak, but much harder than Walnut, Cherry, and most Maples."

Why this matters (QRG): "Website transparency: clear ownership, contact info" is listed directly under Trust indicators, and the QRG treats missing accountability on a transactional page as a Low-quality signal.

  • Identity and contact transparency are complete for a transactional page. A full street address, two purpose-separated email addresses, a newsletter consent disclosure naming the legal entity and its address, and the order phone number rendered twice in body copy — in the opening paragraph, "start your order today at 1-800-253-2728", and in the closing line, "If you want to call to order red oak flooring, dial 1-800-253-2728."

Why this matters (QRG): "Outdated information presented as current" is listed under Untrustworthy Content, and freshness is an explicit Needs Met input. This page clears both, and the title/H1 split means the first thing a visitor reads confirms the click without repeating it verbatim.

  • The page is current, and its title and H1 are correctly differentiated. The CollectionPage node in the HTML audit carries a dateModified of 2026-09-21 15:19:47, two days before capture; the footer reads "© 2026 ReallyCheapFloors.com™ - Copyright."; and the prose is written to the current year throughout, as in "Why red oak is still the go-to choice in 2026". The title tag ("Red Oak Flooring - Red Oak Hardwood Flooring On Sale") and the single H1 ("Red Oak Hardwood Flooring") differ, so the SERP snippet and the on-page headline each do their own job instead of duplicating one another.

What Could Be Improved

Fix: Split the two numbers and label them. Keep the $4.50–$10.00 figure but attribute it explicitly as the national retail range for red oak, then introduce the picks as the liquidation range. For example: nationally, red oak materials run $4.50 to $10.00 per square foot; here is what the same species costs on our floor today, $1.29 to $5.61. That single edit turns a contradiction into the strongest selling argument on the page.

  • The page's own "real product page prices" all fall below the price floor it states two paragraphs earlier. Under its price-examples section the page asserts "Red oak materials cost between $4.50 and $10.00 per square foot." and repeats it as "Red oak materials often land around $4.50 to $10.00 per square foot". Every one of the seven picks then listed under "Example picks (with real product page prices)" is cheaper than that floor, running from "Blue Label: $1.29" up to $3.49. A buyer reading top to bottom is told the market floor is $4.50 and is then shown seven products at a third of it.

Fix: Audit the single SKU feeding that bucket — most likely a zero or placeholder price on a discontinued or call-for-price item — and either restore its real price or exclude null-priced SKUs from facet generation. This is the same defect seen on the Waterproof category, where a "$0.00 - $0.98 (4)" bucket sits above a cheapest product of $1.49, so fix it once at the facet layer rather than page by page.

  • The price facet advertises a bucket that no product on the page can fill. The live Price filter offers "$0.00 - $0.98 (1)", meaning one SKU priced under a dollar. The cheapest price named anywhere on this page — across the twelve-product grid and the full editorial price list — is "Blue Label: $1.29", and the next bucket up, "$1.00 - $1.98 (4)", already accounts for the sub-$2.00 inventory. The shopper who clicks the cheapest bucket on a page branded around the idea that "cheap flooring is our middle name" is the most motivated visitor this page has, and that bucket is the one that cannot deliver.

Fix: Pull these prices from the same source that feeds the grid, or drop the hard-coded figures and let the product cards carry price on their own. If a hand-maintained list is kept, put it on the same review cycle as the sale calendar. A guide that misprices its own product by thirty cents is a refund conversation at the till, and on a page that promises the best price per square foot it is the claim a competitor will screenshot.

  • The editorial price for the Oak Lakes 4-inch does not match the price the grid shows for the same product. The guide lists that product at $3.29. The product card directly above it on the same screen shows a "SALE PRICE:" of "$2.99" against a "Price:" of "$3.49". Neither figure is $3.29. The 5-inch version of the same product is listed correctly at $3.29, which is exactly what a copy-paste between two adjacent lines looks like.

Fix: Normalise the species attribute at the catalogue level so the uppercase variant folds into "Oak", then decide whether "Oak" and "Red Oak" are genuinely different values here. If all 51 oak products are red oak, collapse them and drop the species facet from this category entirely, because a filter that every product matches is noise. Re-categorise or remove the single white oak SKU.

  • The species facet fragments the page's own subject into four buckets, one of which is the wrong species. The Species filter reads "Oak (31)", "Red Oak (12)", "White Oak (1)" and "OAK (8)". A buyer who lands on a page headed "Red Oak Hardwood Flooring" and filters by the species the page is named for sees 12 of the 52 items the grid reports. "Oak (31)" and "OAK (8)" are the same value differing only in capitalisation, and a white oak product should not be in a red oak collection at all.

Fix: Give each statistic a complete sentence and a dated, linked source, in the form: U.S. hardwood flooring sales fell 3.8% from 2024, per [named industry body, year]. Remove the ellipsis and quote the HomeAdvisor line in full with the year of the estimate. The page already links out correctly to the Arbor Day Foundation, so the pattern exists in-house — apply it to the numbers, which are the claims a buyer actually weighs.

  • Two statistics are presented as sourced evidence but cannot be checked, and a third has no figure at all. One callout reads, in full, "That’s a 3.8% decrease from 2024" — a decrease in what is never stated, because the sentence has no subject and nothing above it supplies one. A second is quoted with an ellipsis standing in for the missing attribution: "estimates that it costs an average of $3,162 to install new flooring in a standard 320-square-foot living room (20 feet by 16 feet)". Elsewhere the page asserts that "Recent industry numbers show hardwood demand has been cooling" without naming a number or a source.

Fix: Name both warehouses in the freight paragraph and state the consequence plainly: we ship red oak from Murphy, NC and Dickson, TN, and your rate depends on which one holds your item, shown on the product page before you order. Then repair the broken sentence and the typo. Note also the verified sitewide tel: defect — two different numbers are wired into tel: hrefs across this site, 18002532728 and 18288822722 — so the number a mobile visitor dials may not be the number rendered here. The href values are not exposed in this page's extract, so confirm against the live DOM before that fix ships.

  • More than half the catalogue ships from a warehouse the page never mentions, and one sentence does not parse. The Location facet reads "Murphy, NC (23)" and "Dickson, TN (29)", so 29 of the 52 items ship from Tennessee, while the only address the page discloses is the Murphy, NC warehouse. On a freight-heavy purchase, shipping origin is a cost the buyer needs before checkout, not after. Separately, one sentence in the durability section is broken mid-thought — "If you pair a solid oak hardwood is known to last for decades with a high-quality finish." — and a typo in the opening section compounds the impression, describing "trending-upword white oak".

Verdict

This page reaches High on the QRG Page Quality scale, at the lower edge of that band. The MC is High-quality on the QRG's own terms — original, effortful, technically correct and willing to talk a buyer out of a product — and contact transparency is complete, which is what carries it clear of Medium. For its likely query, red oak hardwood flooring, it Highly Meets the Do intent, with all 52 items reachable across the five paginated pages, and Moderately Meets the Know intent behind how to buy red oak, where the unsourced statistics and the missing wear-layer guidance leave real gaps. The single named drag on the score is accuracy: three unreconciled price contradictions between the prose, the product grid and the live facet data, on a page whose entire promise is price. They read as sloppiness rather than deception, so they do not force a Low rating, but on a transactional page they are the finding most likely to cost a sale. Reconcile the price layer and this is an 8 to 9.

NLP Entity Analysis

Content classification is accurate and confident: /Home & Garden/Home Improvement/Flooring at 0.99, with /Business & Industrial/Construction & Maintenance/Building Materials & Supplies at 0.68 as a sensible secondary. There is no misclassification risk here.

Entity salience tells a weaker story. The distribution is flat — the top entity, a bare oak, reaches only 0.0679, and no entity approaches dominance. The compound that matches the page's actual target, red oak flooring, sits at 0.0196 and resolves as OTHER. Type resolution is inconsistent rather than absent: hardwood flooring and Hardwood Flooring both resolve as CONSUMER_GOOD, which is correct, but Red Oak resolves as ORGANIZATION at 0.0098 and Red oak as LOCATION at 0.0062. The same species is read as three different entity classes on one page.

The core problem is fragmentation plus chrome. The species splits across at least eight surface forms, none of which consolidates; meanwhile Page at 0.0294 is the third-highest entity on the page, and SALE PRICE at 0.0164, Red Oak Natural Type at 0.0078 and Width Sort at 0.0073 all place inside the top fifteen. Four separate Price entities occupy the bottom of the table. These are filter and grid artefacts consuming entity budget that should belong to the species. Consolidating casing in the product feed and suppressing filter UI text from the indexable body would free measurable salience for the primary entity.

Verdict

Entity Analysis, Salient Terms and Schema are the three signals holding this page down: the species fragments across eight surface forms and splits its own facet on letter case, one long-tail phrase is inserted 11 times including twice ungrammatically, and 52 priced SKUs plus five question-and-answer pairs reach Google with no Product, Offer or FAQPage markup at all. Set against that are a Strong Goldmine profile and the deepest editorial prose in the nine-page set at 2,324 words, but the two price contradictions against the page's own live facet data are exactly the kind of copy-versus-data mismatch that undercuts the depth the page otherwise earns.

AI Model Consulted: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) · Assessment Date: September 23, 2026

Would an AI Cite This Page?

Partially — and more willingly than any other page in this set.

Depth is judged here on the editorial prose figure of 2,324 words (the ~407 words of filter and sort chrome are template furniture and are not credited as depth). That makes this the deepest page in the nine-page set by a wide margin, and the density is real rather than padded: there are chunks on this page I would retrieve and quote today.

The strongest is the durability passage. "The Janka Hardness Scale rates it at 1290 lbf" is followed immediately by the unit definition — "lbf stands for pounds-force, which is the unit of measurement for the force required to press a 0.444-inch steel ball halfway into a sample of wood" — and then by a comparative frame, "This rating is a bit softer than white oak, but much harder than Walnut, Cherry, and most Maples." That is a textbook high-citation-probability chunk: a specific number, an expert definition and a comparison, all inside a single span a 200–1,000 token chunker will keep intact. For a query like what is the Janka hardness of red oak flooring, this chunk survives reranking because it answers the question directly instead of circling it.

The supply-and-demand explanation is the second citable unit. "The law of supply and demand is a major factor in the annual sale of red oak hardwood." … "Flooring companies pay more for white oak than red so the price will be lower in general." That is a causal mechanism, not a platitude, and it is the kind of nuanced position the framework flags as distinctive. There is also one properly attributed external statistic — "HomeAdvisor ... estimates that it costs an average of $3,162 to install new flooring in a standard 320-square-foot living room (20 feet by 16 feet)" — which carries a named source, a figure and a defined denominator.

What holds the page back from a full yes is verifiability, not depth. Three things a citation-selection step would catch.

First, the page's own price claim contradicts its own live facet data. The prose states "Red oak materials cost between $4.50 and $10.00 per square foot." and repeats it as "Red oak materials often land around $4.50 to $10.00 per square foot". The price facet on the same screen reads "$0.00 - $0.98 (1)", "$1.00 - $1.98 (4)", "$2.00 - $2.98 (12)" and "$3.00 - $3.98 (6)" — at least 23 of the 52 products are priced below $4.00 — and the top bucket on the page is "$7.00 - $7.98 (3)", so nothing in the catalogue reaches $10.00 either. The page then undercuts itself a third time: every one of the seven entries under "Example picks (with real product page prices)" is priced below $4.50, from "$1.29" to "$3.49".

Second, there is a dangling statistic with no subject and no source. Under the plain-text label "Did You Know?" the page says only "That’s a 3.8% decrease from 2024" — a decrease in what is never stated. The nearest supporting sentence is itself an anonymous-authority anti-pattern: "Recent industry numbers show hardwood demand has been cooling".

Third, an individual product price in the prose disagrees with that same product's grid tile. The budget bullet lists the 4-inch Oak Lakes Cabin at "$3.29", while the "Oak Lakes" tile for that width shows a "SALE PRICE:" of "$2.99" against a "Price:" of "$3.49" — the prose figure matches neither.

Because the answer is Partially, here is what the missing citable content should look like for this client. Consider adding: a sourced, dated demand figure to replace the orphan, and a price claim that matches the catalogue.

Example: "U.S. hardwood flooring shipments fell 3.8% from 2024 to 2025, according to the National Wood Flooring Association 2026 State of the Industry report. Across the 52 red oak SKUs we currently stock, prices run from $1.29 to $7.98 per square foot, with 23 SKUs under $4.00."

Retrieval & Chunking Quality

Chunking is good in the editorial half and poor in the top half, and the two halves behave very differently.

The editorial body chunks cleanly. The heading spine runs 3 H2, 21 H3 and 16 H4, and the descriptive headings are unusually well formed for standalone passage context — "Real price examples: what you pay for red oak in 2026", "Where to shop: get real discounts, not showroom pricing", "Our Best Flooring Options by Buyer Type (2026)". Each front-loads its topic and each governs a self-contained 150–300 word unit, which is close to the ideal chunk size. The five FAQ H4s are literal questions — "Is red oak hardwood flooring worth it in 2026?" — so those chunks reach the reranker already shaped like the query they should match, and the body reinforces the pattern with "What’s the best way to buy red oak hardwood flooring in 2026?".

Two structural gaps break that spine. Eight of the 21 H3s are not content at all — "Price filter", "Species filter", "Grade filter" and the rest of the facet rail — so a heading-driven chunker opens eight near-empty sections before it reaches a single editorial sentence. And the two most quotable callouts have no heading of their own: "Red Oak Buying Guide" and "Did You Know?" render as plain body text rather than H-tags, so the buying-guide preamble and both statistics get absorbed into whatever chunk precedes them instead of becoming their own retrievable units.

Position bias works against the page. Everything an LLM would actually cite sits below the 12-product grid. The first material a chunker meets after the H1 intro is the facet rail and twelve repetitions of "SALE PRICE:", "Price:", "Width:", "Grade:", "Color Name:" and "Type:" — high-frequency, low-information tokens that embed indistinguishably from any other catalogue page. Page-level embedding quality is dragged toward generic ecommerce grid by roughly 400 words of chrome before the distinctive prose gets a chance to pull it back.

Embedding distinctiveness within the prose is genuinely strong in places and self-sabotaged in others. The grade taxonomy is a real semantic anchor — "Utility (3)", "1st Quality (32)", "Cabin (3)", "Blue Label (2)" — and "Buying our Blue Label cabin grade gives you the exact same material and finish as 1st Quality for a fraction of the cost." is a proprietary, contrarian claim that exists almost nowhere else. Against that, the exact six-word string "red oak hardwood flooring buying guide" appears 11 times in 2,324 editorial words, which flattens the embedding toward one repeated n-gram and produces sentences no human wrote: "In practical terms, red oak hardwood flooring buying guide buyers pick it for:" and "In a red oak hardwood flooring buying guide , finish choice is a lifestyle choice."

Retrieval reachability itself is fine. The grid reports "Items 1 - 12 of 52" with numbered pagination, so all 52 SKUs are reachable and no inventory is stranded behind the default view.

What Works

RAG Impact: This stacks the framework's highest-value citation signals three deep — specific data point, expert definition, comparison data — inside a single chunk. A cross-encoder reranker scores it highly for janka rating red oak because the chunk answers the query completely without needing neighbouring context, which is exactly the information-completeness criterion reranking rewards.

  • One genuinely citable hard data point, delivered with its own unit definition. "The Janka Hardness Scale rates it at 1290 lbf" is followed by "lbf stands for pounds-force, which is the unit of measurement for the force required to press a 0.444-inch steel ball halfway into a sample of wood", then placed in context: "This rating is a bit softer than white oak, but much harder than Walnut, Cherry, and most Maples."

RAG Impact: Query-shaped headings put the chunk embedding and the query embedding in nearly the same vector neighbourhood, which is the cheapest available lift to top-K retrieval probability. It also hands the generation step an answer-first passage it can quote without rewriting, which is what citation attribution needs.

  • Question-shaped headings across the whole editorial body, with direct answers underneath. Five H4s are literal user questions, including "What is the best way to buy red oak flooring without overpaying?" and "Should I choose solid oak or engineered oak in 2026?", each followed immediately by a plain-language answer rather than a preamble.

RAG Impact: Freshness is an explicit reranking input. Because the visible copy, the footer year and the structured dateModified all agree, the page avoids the date-manipulation trust anti-pattern that penalises content whose stamped date and body copy disagree.

  • Freshness is internally consistent and machine-confirmable. The prose is dated throughout — "in 2026" appears 19 times, including in headings such as "Our Best Flooring Options by Buyer Type (2026)" — the footer reads "© 2026 ReallyCheapFloors.com", and the CollectionPage node carries a dateModified of 2026-09-21 15:19:47.

RAG Impact: Named frameworks create unique semantic anchors that nothing else in the index competes for, so a query containing the term retrieves this page close to deterministically. The outbound link to a recognised authority is a trust signal that separates the page from purely promotional competitors, which the framework lists as content LLMs will not cite.

  • A named proprietary framework plus a real external authority link. "Blue Label" is a defined product tier with a stated rationale — "Most stores flat-out refuse to carry Blue Label because the profit margins are thin." — and the page closes by pointing outward: "Learn more about the Northern Red Oak from the Arbor Day Foundation".

RAG Impact: A correctly self-referencing @id plus a clean breadcrumb chain tells a retrieval system unambiguously which entity a passage describes and where it sits in the site hierarchy, which improves attribution accuracy when a model cites the page by name rather than by raw URL.

  • Entity identity is clean at the title and schema level. The title tag "Red Oak Flooring - Red Oak Hardwood Flooring On Sale" and the H1 "Red Oak Hardwood Flooring" differ rather than duplicating each other, and the CollectionPage node's @id and url both self-reference this exact URL, supported by a correct three-step BreadcrumbList running Home, Products, Red Oak.

What Could Be Improved

Keep the national installed-cost figure separate and label it as installed rather than material. Example: "Red oak material on this page runs $1.29 to $7.98 per square foot across 52 in-stock SKUs, and 23 of them are under $4.00. Installed is a different number: HomeAdvisor puts an average 320-square-foot living room at $3,162."

  • The stated price range contradicts the page's own live price facet and its own example list. The prose says "Red oak materials cost between $4.50 and $10.00 per square foot." The facet on the same screen reads "$0.00 - $0.98 (1)", "$1.00 - $1.98 (4)", "$2.00 - $2.98 (12)" and "$3.00 - $3.98 (6)" — at least 23 of 52 products below $4.00 — and tops out at "$7.00 - $7.98 (3)". Every entry under "Example picks (with real product page prices)" also falls below $4.50.

Fix: Normalise the species attribute so every red oak SKU carries one "Red Oak" value, merge the case-duplicated option, and move the white oak SKU off this category. The facet count and the H1 should assert the same entity, because an entity extractor reads both. Example: "Red Oak (51) — every board on this page is North American red oak, stocked in Murphy, NC and Dickson, TN. Looking for white oak? See our White Oak collection."

  • The species facet contradicts the page's own premise and splits one attribute across two values. On a page headed "Red Oak Hardwood Flooring" whose intro promises "Discover our wide selection of red oak for sale", the species filter reads "Oak (31)", "Red Oak (12)", "White Oak (1)" and "OAK (8)" — only 12 of the 52 products are tagged as red oak, one is tagged white oak, and the same value is duplicated by letter case.

Fix: Give the figure a subject, a named source and a date, or delete it. An unattributable number is worse than no number, because it trips the unsourced-claim filter and suppresses confidence in the surrounding chunk as well. Example: "U.S. hardwood flooring sales volume fell 3.8% between 2024 and 2025, according to the National Wood Flooring Association 2026 State of the Industry report, which is why liquidated inventory is unusually cheap right now."

  • A statistic with no subject and no source, propped up by an anonymous-authority sentence. The callout reads in full "That’s a 3.8% decrease from 2024" with no antecedent, so a decrease in what is never stated, and the nearest support is "Recent industry numbers show hardwood demand has been cooling", which names no industry body, no report and no year.

Fix: Emit FAQPage over the five questions that already exist, and an ItemList of Product nodes with Offer price and availability built from the attributes already rendered on each tile. The content is there; only the machine-readable layer is missing, so this is a template change rather than a writing job. Example: A Product node reading name "Oak Lakes", material "Red Oak", width "5", grade "Cabin", offers price 3.29, priceCurrency USD, availability InStock, and a FAQPage Question node using the existing "Is red oak hardwood flooring worth it in 2026?" with its existing answer text.

  • No FAQPage, Product, ItemList or Offer node, despite five question-and-answer pairs and 52 priced products. The HTML audit confirms only SiteNavigationElement, CollectionPage, BreadcrumbList and WebSite, with FAQPage marked No and zero FAQ-class elements, yet the page renders a "Frequently Asked Questions" block of five Q&A pairs and a grid whose tiles each carry "Price:", "Width:", "Grade:", "Color Name:" and "Type:".

Fix: Cut to two or three uses, in the intro and the conclusion, and let the H3 spine carry the topic. Replace the rest with the concrete nouns that actually differentiate this page: grade names, plank widths, Janka numbers, warehouse locations. Example: "In practical terms, buyers choose red oak for three reasons: warm pinkish-red undertones, a prominent grain that hides wear, and a Janka rating of 1290 lbf that handles family traffic without denting like walnut."

  • Exact-phrase repetition flattens the page embedding and breaks the prose. The six-word string "red oak hardwood flooring buying guide" appears 11 times in 2,324 editorial words, producing sentences no reader would quote: "In practical terms, red oak hardwood flooring buying guide buyers pick it for:" and "In a red oak hardwood flooring buying guide , finish choice is a lifestyle choice."

Fix: Repair both sentences and attach a named, credentialled byline with a review date. On an expertise topic, an identifiable author is a direct input to source-reliability scoring, and a garbled sentence in the most citable section is the one that gets skipped. Example: "Reviewed by Dale Hensley, 20-year hardwood buyer at Really Cheap Floors in Murphy, NC. Last updated 21 September 2026. Pair solid red oak with a low-gloss finish and the floor is known to last for decades."

  • Two broken sentences and no named author undercut an otherwise authoritative page. The durability section ends mid-thought — "If you pair a solid oak hardwood is known to last for decades with a high-quality finish." — the prose contains "trending-upword white oak", and the heading claim "Everyone Calls Us for Prefinished Red Oak Floors" is backed by zero review or testimonial elements anywhere on the page.

Verdict

Yes, selectively — this is the one page in the set I would quote today, because the Janka passage, the red-versus-white-oak supply explanation and the named grade taxonomy are specific, self-contained and unavailable in that combination elsewhere. The single highest-leverage change is to reconcile the editorial copy with the page's own live product data: a stated range of "$4.50 and $10.00" sitting directly above a facet that tops out at "$7.00 - $7.98 (3)" is the defect most likely to stop a verification step from trusting anything else on the page.

Under its price-examples section the page asserts "Red oak materials cost between $4.50 and $10.00 per square foot." and repeats it as "Red oak materials often land around $4.50 to $10.00 per square foot". Every one of the seven picks then listed under "Example picks (with real product page prices)" is cheaper than that floor, running from "Blue Label: $1.29" up to $3.49. The live Price filter offers "$0.00 - $0.98 (1)", meaning one SKU priced under a dollar. The shopper who clicks the cheapest bucket on a page branded around the idea that "cheap flooring is our middle name" is the most motivated visitor this page has, and that bucket is the one that cannot deliver.

The guide lists that product at $3.29. The product card directly above it on the same screen shows a "SALE PRICE:" of "$2.99" against a "Price:" of "$3.49". Neither figure is $3.29. The 5-inch version of the same product is listed correctly at $3.29, which is exactly what a copy-paste between two adjacent lines looks like.

YMYL Classification

Not core YMYL. The page's purpose is commercial and transactional — sell hickory flooring from a live 27-SKU catalogue — and flooring choice sits in the QRG's "Unlikely YMYL" band for topic harm.

Two factors push it to the low edge of "May be YMYL" rather than leaving it fully outside. First, financial: this is a large, largely irreversible discretionary purchase, and the page is the point of decision — prices run from "$2.49" to "$7.75" per unit against a Square Footage facet where "0 - 1000 (21)" of 27 SKUs sit, which is enough material for a whole-floor order in the four figures. Second, property consequence: the FAQ gives installation and remediation advice with real money attached — "This increases the risk for the boards to swell and create a cupped floor", remedied by "cranking the HVAC or running a dehumidifier to stabilize the environment". Advice that determines whether a customer's floor cups is advice with a cost of being wrong.

The practical implication under QRG section 3 is a modest elevation of the accuracy and attribution bar, not the strict standard applied to health or finance. That elevation matters here for one reason: the page's own consumer-facing numbers contradict each other, and it makes an unverifiable social-proof claim at exactly the moment a buyer is deciding whether to trust it. Under the QRG, Trust is the central E-E-A-T element and it is judged against the page's own verifiable content — which is where this page loses ground, not on topic sensitivity.

So a buyer being asked for a four-figure commitment is told reviews exist, is shown none, and reads the claim in an ungrammatical sentence signalling that nobody edited it. The site links a "Reviews" destination in its navigation, which makes the omission a merchandising choice rather than a lack of material.

Fix: Decide what American Home is and say it once. If it is Bruce's engineered line, write "Bruce American Home" consistently, drop the "Our", and state the construction (sawn face veneer over a 7-ply core) in the merchandising paragraph as well as the footnote. Then link the name straight to the product so the best-seller claim is one click from being verified. If the warehouse genuinely stocks both a solid American Home and Bruce's engineered line, the page has to name them as two distinct products, because as written the best-selling product on the page is the one a buyer cannot identify.

  • The same collection is sold as solid in one section and as another company's engineered line in the next. Under "Our fastest Selling Hickory Hardwoods" the page states "Our American Home collection is a first quality solid hickory hardwood that is our best value for our customers". Roughly 300 words later, inside the engineered column of the solid-versus-engineered comparison, the footnote reads "Somerset's SolidPlus and Bruce's American Home lines use sawn face veneers". A shopper who reads both cannot tell whether American Home is solid or engineered, or whether it is the retailer's own collection or Bruce's. The page then stakes its strongest merchandising claim on it — "our American Home is easily the most popular and best-selling first quality product in our warehouses" — and no card in the first twelve results is named American Home.

Fix: Move the bucket boundaries onto the price points the catalogue actually uses, so the ranges read $3.00 - $3.99 and $4.00 - $4.99 and a $3.99 hickory appears where a shopper looks for it. While that change is being made, check what the "$0.00 - $0.98 (1)" bucket resolves to and relabel it honestly. An "under $1.00" bucket on a hickory page is the first thing a bargain shopper clicks, and finding a $0.99 product there — or an empty result — is the cheapest possible way to lose a first-time buyer's confidence.

  • The price filter's bucket labels do not contain the prices the page is charging, and the arithmetic proves it. Two products in the visible grid are listed at "$3.99". The buckets offered are "$3.00 - $3.98 (10)" and "$4.00 - $4.98 (2)", and neither contains $3.99. The counts force the conclusion: the seven buckets sum to exactly 27, matching "Items 1 - 12 of 27"; "$4.00 - $4.98 (2)" is already fully accounted for by the two visible items at $4.19 and $4.29, and "$2.00 - $2.98 (1)" by the single $2.69. That leaves the two $3.99 items being counted inside a bucket whose label tops out at $3.98. Every boundary on this facet ends in .98 while the catalogue's prices end in .9, so the mislabel runs through the whole filter — including "$0.00 - $0.98 (1)", which on the same pattern will resolve to a $0.99 floor rather than a sub-dollar one.

Fix: Either stock the recommendation or reframe it. If engineered hickory is genuinely one SKU, say so where the advice is given: name that product, link it, and add an honest alternative — that a narrower solid plank in a climate-controlled room is the better bet here, and that the free sample programme exists to settle it. The page already models this candour elsewhere with "the occasional wide plank options we get in stock", and the FAQ should match it.

  • The page's central recommendation points at an inventory of one. The FAQ presents engineered as the answer to hickory's defining weakness, twice: "Engineered flooring exists specifically to solve hickory's stability issues." and "The common remedy to this is to purchase a prefinished engineered plank hickory for increased stability, especially if you are looking for a wider size for your selected room." The Type facet reads "Engineered (1)" against "Prefinished Solid (26)", and the widest option in the Width facet is "7.5 (1)". The body copy reinforces the expectation — "Shopping solid or engineered hickory will give a customer the strongest wood grown in America underfoot" and "The demand for Cabin grade Hickory flooring in both solid and engineered is very high." — so a reader persuaded by the argument arrives at a single-item result and concludes the site is out of stock rather than that it never stocked it.

Fix: Put a name on the opinion. A short signature block under "What Grade is Best For Me?" giving a named buyer or installer, their years in the trade, the Murphy or Dickson warehouse they work out of, and a photo converts an anonymous "in my opinion" into the everyday expertise the QRG explicitly accepts, and it costs nothing to add because the person already exists. Then give the copy one editing pass: fix "undenailable", rewrite the two garbled Janka sentences, and decide whether the folksy register stays. Either choice works, but the current mix reads as unreviewed.

  • Unedited prose and an unsigned first-person opinion undercut a genuinely knowledgeable page. "Hickory brings a special rustic visual that is both unique and undenailable" carries a typo in a headline sentence. "All domestic hardwoods like white oak, red oak, and even walnut are put through a universal lab coat environment test" is not a sentence a flooring professional would leave standing, and "A Janka test is meant to settle once and for all what the difference in hardness between each plentiful wood species we have found in the wild." is ungrammatical. Registers collide inside single sections, with "You darn tootin' it is." and "However, Momma will ask if you can sand and refinish this battered hardwood to make her feel better." sitting beside real technical exposition. Meanwhile the most authoritative line on the page — "Hickory, more than any other wood in my opinion, offers very different looks between grades." — is attributed to nobody: there is no byline, no author block and no named person anywhere on it.

Fix: Finish the comparison in a small table beside the existing solid-versus-engineered one: hickory's Janka figure against red oak, white oak and walnut, with the source named underneath. Then tie it to the catalogue rather than to an abstraction — name which Cabin grade product on this page is the one to put in a mudroom with kids and a dog. Consider adding: the rating figure itself inside "Why Choose Hickory Hardwood?", since it is the strongest selling point the page has and it is currently described rather than stated.

  • The page explains the Janka test at length and never gives hickory's number. It sets the measurement up across three paragraphs, then asserts "Hickory has the highest domestic wood Janka rating." and "This beastly rating is why hickory flooring is positioned as a superior choice compared to oak or any other species of wood when long-term durability is the main focus." — without stating the rating, without stating what oak scores, and without citing a source. It names the comparison species ("white oak, red oak, and even walnut") but never makes the comparison, so the one hard fact a shopper came to check is the one fact withheld.

Verdict

This page earns a Medium Page Quality rating under the QRG, at the top of that band: the Main Content is 1,593 words of original, opinionated operator writing backed by a stated 50-year installation history, a six-question FAQ that leads with the product's downsides, a solid-versus-engineered comparison table, and 27 fully specified SKUs all reachable by following links, with six of seven facets reconciling exactly to the catalogue and with business identity, contact routes, policies and freshness fully disclosed.

What holds it out of High is Trustworthiness rather than content quality, and specifically the gap between what the page says and what the page's own data shows: five-star reviews claimed against 0 review elements, a best-selling collection described as solid in one section and as Bruce's engineered line in the next, an engineered remedy recommended twice against an "Engineered (1)" facet, and a price filter whose labels provably exclude the "$3.99" products it is counting. Against Needs Met for a transactional query such as hickory hardwood flooring or cheap hickory flooring, this lands at Highly Meets — the buyer sees real, priced, filterable inventory and a phone number to close on. For the research intent behind is hickory flooring worth it or solid vs engineered hickory it sits at Moderately Meets: the answers are genuinely good, but they are unsigned, the headline Janka figure is never given, and the contradictions a careful reader will notice are reason enough to go and check somewhere else.
