NLP Entity Analysis

Google NLP classifies the page /Home & Garden/Home Improvement/Flooring at 0.98 confidence, with /Business & Industrial/Construction & Maintenance/Building Materials & Supplies at 0.56. That is the correct vertical at near-certainty, and it is the cleanest classification signal on the page.

The headline win is entity grounding. "White Oak" now resolves to the Wikipedia entity Quercus alba, meaning Google is matching the page to a real node in the Knowledge Graph rather than to a character string. "USA" likewise resolves to the United States node, supporting the made-in-America positioning. "Hardwood Flooring" types correctly as CONSUMER_GOOD.

Salience distribution is where the page still loses. The ranking runs oak (0.0395, OTHER), "Oak Price" (0.0319, OTHER), "Hardwood Flooring" (0.0287), "Page" (0.0275, OTHER), then "White Oak" (0.0208). Two of the four entities above the page subject are interface artefacts produced by the product grid and the pagination control, not content. Below that, a run of near-identical 0.0091 entries covers "Price filter", "Layer filter", "Footage filter", "Location filter" and "Grade filter", all harvested from the faceted navigation. Type resolution is imprecise: "White Oak" and "Euro White Oak" both type as LOCATION, and "Red Oak" types as ORGANIZATION.

The practical reading is that the entity budget is being shared with the template. Dilution is materially reduced from the prior assessment and the subject is now Knowledge Graph linked, but the page subject does not yet dominate its own entity profile.

What Works

Signal: US10235423B2 scores entity metrics against resolved entities, not strings. Wikipedia-linked resolution is the precondition for the page competing on topical authority for the species term at all.

  • The primary entity resolves to a real Knowledge Graph node. NLP maps "White Oak" to Quercus alba, and "USA" to the United States entity, so the page is understood as being about a specific hardwood species rather than about a two-word phrase.

Signal: Goldmine penalises titles that the page body or headings contradict. Total agreement across every high-weight position drives percentBodyTitleTokensCovered up and suppresses title rewrite risk.

  • Title, H1, canonical, breadcrumb and schema name all agree. The HTML audit confirms a single H1 reading "White Oak Hardwood Flooring", an exactly matching title tag, a self-referencing canonical, and a CollectionPage node whose @id and url both point at this URL.

Signal: NavBoost rewards lastLongestClicks. A user who lands and can actually reach the full assortment has a reason to stay in-session rather than returning to the SERP for a fuller competitor listing.

  • All 31 SKUs are reachable and the count is stated on the page. The grid reports "Items 1 - 12 of 31" with pagination to pages 2 and 3, giving 36 slots for 31 products, so no inventory is stranded behind a broken control.

Signal: The 4-timestamp system cross-references bylineDate against contentage and lastSignificantUpdate specifically to catch date-bumping. Here all four agree, so the recency claim is credible instead of suspect.

  • The freshness timestamps corroborate rather than conflict. dateModified reads 2026-09-18 against a 2024-07-17 publish date, the footer reads "© 2026 ReallyCheapFloors.com", and the prose independently dates itself to 2026.

Signal: US11409748B1 indexes and ranks at passage level. Question-form headings with self-contained answers are the exact shape the passage ranker and the featured snippet systems extract.

  • The FAQ block is written as real question-and-answer passages. Three H3s in natural question form, including "Are white oak floors expensive?", each followed by a substantive answer containing a specific figure.

What Could Be Improved

Fix: Rewrite the claim to the range the facet actually supports, for example white oak starting at $0.99 per square foot with most of the range landing between $2 and $5. A shopper who scrolls two inches sees the contradiction, and on price-led queries such as cheap white oak flooring under $3 that mismatch is a badClicks generator. Accurate ranges also let the price facet and the copy reinforce one instead of undercutting each other.

  • The page's own price facet contradicts its headline price promise, twice. The copy claims "prices well under $3 per square foot" and the FAQ states the flooring "costs less than $3 per square foot". The live price filter on the same screen reads "$4.00 - $4.98 (9)" plus five more products in the $5 band and three in the $7 band, so 20 of the 31 products are priced at $3.00 or above. Three of the four prefinished solid products actually visible in the grid are above $4.80, including "Dundee Plank LG" at "$5.61".

Fix: Point the wide-plank copy at the widths actually stocked, 7, 7.25, 7.5 and 8.25, and move genuine 12-inch demand to the Wide Plank Flooring category where it can be answered. Attracting a query the assortment cannot satisfy is the cleanest form of pogo-sticking there is.

  • The page invites 12-inch-wide plank searches it cannot serve. The copy opens a section with "Looking for 12 inch width hardwood" and later promises "board lengths from 12 inches wide to 7 feet in length", but the Width filter lists a maximum of 8.25 and nothing between 8.25 and 12.

Fix: Either state the figure the facets support or scope the claim to total white oak inventory across the warehouse rather than to this page's assortment. contentEffort rewards verifiable specifics; a specific number the page itself refutes is worse than no number.

  • The inventory figure exceeds what the square footage facet can hold. The copy claims "over 400,000 square feet of prefinished white oak flooring". The Square Footage filter reports "0 - 10000 (29)" and "10000 - 20000 (2)", which caps the entire assortment at roughly 330,000 square feet even if every product sat at the top of its bucket, and only 14 of the 31 products are tagged Prefinished Solid against "Engineered (17)".

Fix: Add an ItemList of Product nodes with Offer price, priceCurrency and availability drawn from the same data that already feeds the grid, plus FAQPage markup on the three existing questions. The structured attributes the filters already expose, price, width, grade, species, are exactly what qualifies a category page for search filter chips and rich product results.

  • Priced products and answered questions are both left unmarked in schema. The HTML audit confirms only SiteNavigationElement, CollectionPage, BreadcrumbList and WebSite, with FAQPage explicitly absent, despite 31 products carrying visible prices, widths, grades and types, and three question-form H3s with full answers.

Fix: Render the filter group labels as styled spans or divs rather than H3s, and promote the inventory section to H2 in the editorial sequence. That removes eight non-topical nodes from the vectorized heading path and puts an inventory-intent heading back at the level Google weights.

  • The heading vector is half filter chrome. Eight of the thirteen H3s the HTML audit records are interface labels such as "Price filter" sitting under the "Shop By" H2, and the genuine inventory topic "A Huge Inventory of Hardwood Floor Products" is demoted to H3 beneath an unrelated appearance section.

Fix: Align the copy to the grade vocabulary the store actually uses, and retag the 16 generically-tagged Oak products to their true species so the Species facet resolves to white oak for the pages that claim it. Consistent attribute vocabulary between copy, facet and schema is what lets the same term reinforce across the body and structured-data channels instead of splitting weight.

  • A grade named in the copy does not exist in the grade facet. The prose reassures buyers that "Even our #1 Common grades maintain excellent consistency", but the live Grade filter offers only 1st Quality, 1st Quality Discontinued, Blue Label, Shorts and Builder A, with "1st Quality (22)" dominating. Separately, the Species facet shows "White Oak (12)" and "Euro White Oak (2)" against "Oak (16)" and even "Red Oak (1)" on a page titled for white oak.

Fix: Emit og:title, og:description, og:image and og:url plus twitter:card on the category template, reusing the existing meta description and the lead product image. Cheap to ship once, and it protects the click quality of every social and messaging-app share, which is a real acquisition path for a discount flooring buyer sending options to a spouse or contractor.

  • Zero Open Graph and zero Twitter Card tags. The HTML audit records OG Description as NONE, and no Twitter Card tags exist, so every share of this URL renders without a controlled title, description or image.

Fix: Strip the fragment from the pagination template. Nothing is stranded, since all 31 products remain reachable, but the fragment is a leftover from a review template and it sends the browser hunting for an anchor that was never rendered.

  • Every pagination link targets a fragment that does not exist. The pagination controls append #customer-review-list, an anchor present nowhere in the DOM, to pages 2 and 3.

Verdict

Entity grounding, title alignment and timestamp consistency are genuine strengths, and the CollectionPage and BreadcrumbList markup is correctly built rather than merely present. The score is held at 6 by the Schema gap, with 31 priced SKUs and three answered questions left entirely unmarked, and by a Content Quality and NavBoost problem the archived HTML could not show: the editorial copy makes price, width, inventory and grade claims that the page's own live facet counts contradict on the same screen.

AI Model Consulted: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) · Assessment Date: September 23, 2026

Would an AI Cite This Page?

Partially. I would retrieve this page for commercial-intent queries and quote from a narrow band of it — but I would not cite it as a factual reference, because the page contradicts its own live data in four separate places, and a reranker that cross-checks a passage against the structured data sitting beside it on the same page will find those conflicts and demote the chunk.

The citable part is real and worth naming first. The three FAQ answers are the only chunks here that behave like reference content: they lead with a claim, explain a mechanism, and carry one verifiable number. "White oak's closed-cell structure makes it naturally more water-resistant than red oak" is a proper causal explanation rather than marketing, and the "1360 Janka rating" appears twice — once in body copy as "With a Janka Hardness rating of 1360" and once inside the FAQ. That is a specific, checkable data point of exactly the kind the citation-selection criteria reward, and it is the strongest retrieval asset on the page.

Everything else fails the reranker for one reason: the editorial prose makes quantitative claims that the page's own filter facets refute, on the same screen.

  • The copy asks "Looking for 12 inch width hardwood to create that modern, seamless aesthetic?" and later offers "board lengths from 12 inches wide to 7 feet in length". The Width filter on the same page tops out at "- 8.25 (1)". No 12-inch width exists in the inventory being described.
  • "Our prefinished oak solid hardwood delivers professional-grade quality with prices well under $3 per square foot!" and the FAQ's "Our USA-made white oak flooring costs less than $3 per square foot" both fail against the Price filter, which counts "- $4.00 - $4.98 (9)", "- $5.00 - $5.98 (5)" and "- $7.00 - $7.98 (3)" — 17 of the 31 products are priced at $4.00 or more, and only 11 fall under $3.00.
  • "Our inventory includes over 400,000 square feet of prefinished white oak flooring in many popular stain colors." The Square Footage filter reads "- 0 - 10000 (29)" and "- 10000 - 20000 (2)". Taking every SKU at the very top of its own bucket, the page's own data caps this collection at roughly 330,000 square feet. The prose claim sits above the ceiling its own facet sets.
  • "Even our #1 Common grades maintain excellent consistency" names a grade the page does not sell. The Grade filter offers "- 1st Quality (22)", "- Blue Label (2)" and "- Builder A (3)", with no #1 Common option anywhere.

That pattern is what caps the score. An LLM asked how wide are Really Cheap Floors white oak planks or how much is white oak flooring per square foot can read both the answer and its refutation inside one retrieved chunk. The safe behaviour is to skip the source.

Concrete citable content this page could carry, written as the client could publish it:

"Our white oak inventory spans 2 1/4 inch strip through 8 1/4 inch wide plank, in solid and engineered construction, priced from $0.99 to $7.98 per square foot."

"White oak rates 1360 on the Janka hardness scale, against 1290 for red oak and 1010 for American black walnut, which is why it resists denting better than either in high-traffic rooms."

"Because white oak's pores are plugged with tyloses, it absorbs far less water than red oak — the same property that makes it the only North American oak used for whiskey and wine barrels."

Each of those is a bounded, checkable statement that survives a cross-check against the product grid, which is precisely what the current copy does not do.

Retrieval & Chunking Quality

Chunking is this page's strongest structural feature. Six descriptive H2s carry the editorial body — "Why White Oak Flooring Is the Smart Choice", "A Superior Hardwood Species That Outlasts the Others", "The USA-Made Quality Difference" — and each is followed by one or two self-contained paragraphs. Chunk boundaries fall on real topic shifts rather than mid-thought, and the headings are descriptive enough to serve as standalone passage context if a chunk is retrieved away from its parent page. The three FAQ H3s are better still: "Are white oak floors expensive?", "Is white oak an expensive wood?" and "What is so special about white oak?" are literal user queries, so the query embedding and the heading embedding land in almost the same place.

Depth is adequate for the chunk count. Judged on the editorial prose figure of 1,075 words — not the 1,543 total, and explicitly excluding the 382 words of filter and sort chrome, which is template furniture and earns no credit as depth — this page sits mid-range for the set, above the 502-word floor and well below the 2,324-word ceiling. Roughly 150 words per editorial section is on the thin side of the 200–300 word target but still substantive enough to chunk cleanly.

Embedding distinctiveness is where it degrades, for three compounding reasons.

First, the page is diluted at the entity level. NLP resolves "White Oak" to the Wikipedia entity Quercus alba, which is a genuine grounding win and means a retriever knows this page is about the tree species rather than a place of the same name. But that entity carries only 0.0208 salience, and two pieces of template chrome outrank it — a price-column artefact at 0.0319 and a pagination label at 0.0275. The most salient strings in this document are furniture, not subject. The dilution is much reduced, but it has not been eliminated.

Second, a large share of the prose produces embeddings that overlap with every other discount-flooring page on the web. "We all want the natural look with a wider plank width" and "This uniformity is exactly what interior designers love." are generic-statement signals: they assert a preference without a source, a number, or anything an embedding can anchor to. "Most of our hardwood is white labeled to present the highest flooring brands products at the lowest price they can allow." is worse — it is close to semantically empty and will not match any real query.

Third, most sections close by drifting into sales copy, which trips the commercial-intent detector in the framework's low-citation table. The repeating pattern is fact, fact, call to action — so the highest-value sentences are reliably followed by the lowest-value ones inside the same chunk, dragging the chunk average down.

Position is handled reasonably. The H1 and the strongest differentiator paragraph sit near the top, and the FAQ block sits at the end, so both high-attention regions carry real content rather than boilerplate. The product grid in the middle is legitimate primary content for a category page, and it reports "Items 1 - 12 of 31" with working pagination, so the full catalogue is reachable rather than stranded.

What Works

RAG Impact: Question-shaped headings put the chunk embedding and the query embedding in near-identical vector space, which is the single biggest lever on initial retrieval. A cross-encoder reranker then rewards the answer for directly answering rather than tangentially relating — the framework's stated reranking criterion. These three chunks are the page's most retrievable passages by a wide margin.

  • The FAQ block is written in the exact question form users type, and the answers actually answer. The three H3s are "Are white oak floors expensive?", "Is white oak an expensive wood?" and "What is so special about white oak?" — matching the real query is white oak flooring expensive almost token for token. The third answer explains a mechanism rather than asserting a preference: "White oak's closed-cell structure makes it naturally more water-resistant than red oak".

RAG Impact: Specific data points are the top entry in the high-citation-probability table, because a model needs a verifiable anchor before it will attribute a claim. A named industry scale plus an exact value gives the page one genuine citation hook on durability queries, and the repetition means the fact survives whichever of the two chunks is retrieved.

  • One hard, verifiable number carries the durability claim, and it is stated twice. "With a Janka Hardness rating of 1360" appears in the body copy and "1360 Janka rating" again inside the FAQ.

RAG Impact: Correct self-referencing identity is what lets a retrieval system attribute a chunk to the right canonical source and reconstruct where the page sits in the site hierarchy. Ambiguous or mismatched @id values are a common cause of a citation being attributed to the wrong URL or dropped altogether; this page does not have that problem.

  • The structured data identifies the page to a retriever correctly. The JSON-LD carries a CollectionPage whose @id and url both self-reference this exact URL, alongside a correct three-step BreadcrumbList running Home, Products, White Oak.

RAG Impact: Labelled attribute blocks parse into structured facts a model can extract and compare, which is far more useful than prose for what widths does X sell style queries. Entity grounding to a Wikipedia node strengthens the page's semantic anchor exactly as the framework's named-entity principle predicts, and it separates this page from thousands of pages that use the phrase loosely.

  • The product grid exposes machine-readable attributes per SKU, and the subject entity resolves to the right thing. Each tile emits labelled fields for price, width, grade, colour name and type, and NLP grounds "White Oak" to Quercus alba, correctly reading it as the species.

What Could Be Improved

Fix: Rewrite every quantitative sentence to state the range the facets actually support, and generate that copy from the same inventory feed that populates the filters so it cannot drift again. On a liquidation model where stock turns constantly, a hand-typed number in prose will always end up contradicting the grid beside it. Example: "Our white oak collection currently runs 31 products from 2 1/4 inch strip to 8 1/4 inch plank, priced $0.99 to $7.98 per square foot, in 1st Quality, Blue Label and Builder A grades — with 11 SKUs under $3.00 today."

  • Four editorial claims are refuted by the page's own filter data, on the same screen. The copy says "Looking for 12 inch width hardwood to create that modern, seamless aesthetic?" against a Width filter topping out at "- 8.25 (1)"; it says "Our prefinished oak solid hardwood delivers professional-grade quality with prices well under $3 per square foot!" against a Price filter counting "- $4.00 - $4.98 (9)", "- $5.00 - $5.98 (5)" and "- $7.00 - $7.98 (3)"; it says "Our inventory includes over 400,000 square feet of prefinished white oak flooring in many popular stain colors." against a Square Footage filter of "- 0 - 10000 (29)" and "- 10000 - 20000 (2)"; and it says "Even our #1 Common grades maintain excellent consistency" against a Grade filter offering only "- 1st Quality (22)", "- Blue Label (2)" and "- Builder A (3)".

Fix: Add FAQPage schema wrapping the three existing H3 questions and their answers verbatim, and emit an ItemList of Product nodes with Offer price and priceCurrency for the grid. No new content has to be written — it is already on the page, simply invisible as structured data to the systems that feed AI answers. Example: A single Offer node reading price $0.99, priceCurrency USD, availability InStock on the "Unfinished Shorts" tile makes that SKU eligible for direct extraction into a shopping answer, where today its price is prose a model has to infer.

  • Three FAQ questions and 31 priced products sit on the page, and none of it is marked up. The HTML audit confirms zero FAQPage schema and zero FAQ-class elements, and the JSON-LD graph carries no Product, ItemList or Offer node despite every tile rendering a price. The page also carries zero Open Graph tags and zero Twitter Card tags.

Fix: Close the two-cent gaps between consecutive bands and generate the edges from the live minimum and maximum price rather than from a fixed ladder. As built, a shopper filtering on the cheapest band either sees nothing or sees a product priced outside the band they selected. Example: Replace the ladder with contiguous bands built from the real range — $0.99 to $1.99, $2.00 to $2.99, $3.00 to $3.99, $4.00 to $4.99, $5.00 to $5.99, and $6.00 and above — so every price on the page falls inside exactly one labelled bucket.

  • The price facet's own bucket labels do not cover the prices in the grid. The ranges run "- $0.00 - $0.98 (1)" through "- $7.00 - $7.98 (3)", and their counts sum to exactly 31, matching "Items 1 - 12 of 31" — so every SKU is bucketed somewhere. Yet the cheapest visible product, "Unfinished Shorts", is priced $0.99, which falls into no advertised range. The ladder also skips the $6.00 to $6.98 band entirely while still offering a $7.00 band above it.

Fix: Name the source behind every hard number, and either attribute the anonymous-expert sentences to a named person or delete them. Add a visible last-reviewed date to the editorial block so freshness can be assessed from the page itself rather than only from the schema. Example: "Janka hardness measured per ASTM D1037. White oak: 1360 lbf. Red oak: 1290 lbf. Hard maple: 1450 lbf. Source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, Chapter 5."

  • Nothing on the page is attributed, and the strongest claims are the least sourced. The Janka figure arrives with no standard or testing body named. "This is often half what competitors charge online." names no competitor and no price. "This uniformity is exactly what interior designers love." is an anonymous-authority construction of precisely the kind the framework flags. The audit records zero review or testimonial signal elements, and the page shows no author and no visible date.

Fix: Populate wear layer on all 17 engineered SKUs, re-tag the 16 generic Oak products to their true species, and make every product name unique by appending the colour name that already exists in the tile data. Example: Render the tile heading as "Ambient Oak — White Oak Natural, 7 inch, Engineered, 3mm wear layer, $3.49/sq ft" so a model asked what does Ambient Oak cost returns one unambiguous answer instead of two conflicting ones.

  • Product specs are incomplete and product names are ambiguous, so extracted facts collide. The Wear Layer filter records only "- 3 mm (6)" and "- 3.5 mm (1)" against a Type filter of "- Engineered (17)", so 10 engineered SKUs publish no wear layer — the primary buying spec for engineered wood. Species tagging on a white oak page reads "- Oak (16)", "- White Oak (12)", "- Euro White Oak (2)" and "- Red Oak (1)", so most products are not tagged to the species the page is about, and one is tagged as the competing species the copy argues against. Duplicate product names compound it: two "Ambient Oak" tiles show $3.49 and $1.69.

Verdict

I would quote the Janka figure and the closed-cell water-resistance explanation out of the FAQ, but I would not cite this page as a reference source, because its own filter data refutes four of its quantitative claims — plank width, price point, inventory volume and grade name — and a page that disagrees with itself in public is a page a reranker drops. The single highest-value change is to regenerate every number in the editorial copy from the same inventory feed that renders the facets, which removes all four contradictions at once and makes the genuinely good FAQ answers safe to cite.

🔴 Critical Fixes — Highest Opportunity

1. The copy invites shoppers to a plank width the page does not sell.
The prose opens a whole section with "Looking for 12 inch width hardwood to create that modern, seamless aesthetic?" and the closing block repeats it as "board lengths from 12 inches wide to 7 feet in length". The page's own Width facet tops out at "8.25 (1)", and its nine width buckets sum to exactly 31 — the full catalogue. Not one of the 31 products is 12 inches wide, and the widest is 8.25.

2. The headline price promise is wrong for the majority of the catalogue.
The body claims "prices well under $3 per square foot!" and the FAQ repeats "Our USA-made white oak flooring costs less than $3 per square foot". The Price facet, which also sums to exactly 31, reads "$4.00 - $4.98 (9)", "$5.00 - $5.98 (5)" and "$7.00 - $7.98 (3)" — 17 of 31 products, 55% of the page, are priced at $4.00 or more, and only 11 of 31 sit under $3. The visible grid confirms it: "Dundee Plank LG" at "$5.61", "Dundee Strip HG" at "$4.81" and a second "Dundee Plank LG" at "$5.06" are all on the first screen, directly above the paragraph making the claim.

3. The inventory-volume claim exceeds what the page's own footage facet can hold.
The copy states "Our inventory includes over 400,000 square feet of prefinished white oak flooring in many popular stain colors." The Square Footage facet reports "0 - 10000 (29)" and "10000 - 20000 (2)", so even if every one of the 31 items sat at the very top of its bucket the arithmetic ceiling is 330,000 square feet, and the realistic total is far below that. The claim also specifies prefinished, while the Type facet reads "Prefinished Solid (14)" against "Engineered (17)", so fewer than half the items on the page are prefinished solid at all.

🟡 Recommended Improvements

1. A product visible on the first screen is priced outside every advertised price bucket.
The seven price buckets sum to 31, so every SKU is counted somewhere, yet "Unfinished Shorts" sits in the grid at "$0.99" — above the top of "$0.00 - $0.98 (1)" and below the floor of "$1.00 - $1.98 (3)". The ladder has a second hole between "$5.00 - $5.98 (5)" and "$7.00 - $7.98 (3)", where nothing covers $6.00 to $6.98.

2. A red oak product is merchandised on the white oak page while the copy argues against red oak.
The Species facet reads "Oak (16)", "White Oak (12)", "Euro White Oak (2)" and "Red Oak (1)". Only 12 of 31 items are tagged as the species named in the H1 "White Oak Hardwood Flooring", 16 are tagged only as generic "Oak", and one is explicitly Red Oak — on a page whose selling argument is that white oak means "fewer knots and color variations than red oak or walnut flooring".

3. Nothing on the page attributes any claim to anyone.
There is no author, no buyer, no expert reviewer and no sourcing behind statements such as "Every plank we sell is manufactured in America under strict quality control standards." or the warranty assurance "We work directly with manufacturers to honor their warranty coverage.", which names no warranty, no term and no manufacturer and links to nothing.

4. The page shows zero social proof while the site navigation promises it.
The HTML audit records 0 review/testimonial signal elements and 0 FAQ-class elements, yet "Reviews" sits in the navigation. A shopper told reviews exist has to leave the category to find them, and returns to a 31-product grid where not one item carries a rating.

5. The grid uses grade jargon it never explains where the jargon is used.
Tiles carry "Blue Label", "Builder A", "Shorts" and "1st Quality Discontinued" as bare labels, and the only explanation sits behind a "Grade Information" link in the top navigation, several clicks from the decision. A first-time buyer cannot tell whether "Blue Label" is better or worse than "Builder A", yet the two differ in price on this page.

✅ What's Already Working

Every SKU in the category is actually reachable.

The species writing is accurate trade knowledge, not filler.

Website transparency is complete for a transactional page.

The primary entity resolves to a real Knowledge Graph node.

Title, H1, canonical, breadcrumb and schema name all agree.

Second, the fold screenshots are rendered from each page's own captured DOM, so layout, headings and facet counts are exactly what was assessed, but product photography is absent because the browser save did not retain the lazy-loaded imagery. This assessment was produced using AI-assisted analysis with human editorial review, against the live site as it stood on 23 September 2026. Because www.reallycheapfloors.com serves a Cloudflare managed challenge that returns HTTP 403 to automated requests, each page was captured by hand in a real browser on that date and assessed from the saved rendered DOM. Structural findings (heading tags, canonical, schema, link and image counts, word counts) were read from that captured HTML directly, and NLP entity data was extracted from the same capture via the Google Cloud Natural Language API. Because the capture is post-JavaScript, the product counts shown in each category's filter rail are included in the evidence base, and several findings in this report compare those live counts against the editorial copy beside them.
